posts.title: 99 For Founders is Back
posts.description: One of the greatest and most humbling lessons my dad taught me as a kid was: “A smart person learns from their own mistakes. A smarter person learns the mistakes of others.” Paired nicely with another piece of wisdom he spoke to often: “A smart person stands on the shoulders of giants.” Learn from others. As often as you can. As broadly and as deeply as you can. They’re both lessons that have stayed with me till this day. Both of which also gave birth to the 99 series . A total of 297 lessons each for founders and investors. (For now). Gathered from people smarter than me. Who have walked different paths than I have. Who have earned scar tissue where I have not, have yet to, and hope to not. I never know how long each set of 99 pieces of advice would take to collect. Some series, in a smattering of months. posts.title: Risk is Defined by 4 Words
posts.description: This is more or less Part Dos of the risk framework I shared last year with my buddy Benjamin . What LPs define as risk when investing in GPs. This one, unlike the last, is my own Shakespearean (or lack thereof) interpretation. How I underwrite risk in GPs. So, a/ this is not the Bible, b/ use your own best judgment, c/ if you don’t know where to start, hopefully this serves as inspiration. After I read the deck and meet with a GP once, I write a list of all the risks I can think of about said GP. Then I stack rank them in the order of most to least important (to me). Obviously a subjective take. Then draw a line in there that determines the least amount of risk I’m willing to tolerate before investing. Then I do references and homework to see if I can alleviate the top risks of investing. Sometimes that means more conversations with the GP. Sometimes that means talking to others. posts.title: Creativity starts at 2 degrees
posts.description: One degree of freedom removed from the status quo is what most people, even if they can’t do, can imagine. And because they can imagine it—”I could have come up with that idea myself”—what you have doesn’t feel innovative. They may ask you “why” once, but they’ll get to the answer they expect to hear pretty quickly. Starting at two degrees of freedom removed, you start at the imagination’s imagination. The fringe of the fringe, so to speak. Then, by most people’s standards, you are creative. Not one standard deviation but two standard deviations from the mean. Which starts putting you in the uncommon 5%. It’s where the average person starts calling you “built different”. I don’t know if that phrase means anything if it’s overused or used by people who refuse, for whatever reason, to be different themselves.
